source: Original KaiSip study notes, organized by The IIA's CIA Part 3 syllabus effective 2025. KaiSip is an independent study aid, not affiliated with or endorsed by The IIA.
overview: Section A is the chief audit executive's management desk: how the internal audit function is organized, funded, staffed, equipped and steered over several years, and how its head keeps the board and senior management informed. It draws mainly on Domain IV of the Standards and on Principle 8, Overseen by the Board. On exam questions the chief audit executive proposes, manages and reports; the board approves the charter, plan, budget and resource plan; senior management gives input and support.
analogy: Think of the head chef who runs a restaurant kitchen for its owners. The chef sets a few years' vision for the menu, proposes the kitchen budget, hires and trains cooks, decides when to bring in an outside caterer, buys equipment and teaches the cooks to use it, and rewrites the kitchen's procedures when the health code changes. The owners approve the money and the season's menu, hear promptly when deliveries are cut, and meet the chef alone now and then. The chef answers for every plate, even one the caterer cooked.

topics.overview: Running the function day to day means deciding who does the work (staff, an outside firm or both), watching how the work is going, setting the mix of assurance and advisory engagements, and keeping the written methods current. The chief audit executive owns each of these, even when an outside provider does the work.
can_do: Describe how the chief audit executive oversees outside firms doing internal audit work, and what stays with the chief audit executive
Describe the tools that show how the function's work is going, from supervision to budget variance
Describe how the plan's mix of assurance and advisory work is set, and when a change must reach the board
Identify the events that should prompt a review of the function's methodologies

subtopics.name: Managing External Service Providers
subtopics.definition: Managing external service providers means choosing, contracting, supervising and reviewing outside firms that do internal audit work; the chief audit executive (CAE) keeps responsibility for results.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Outsourcing buys skills or capacity, not a handover of duty: the Standards bind contracted auditors in full, and the board still oversees the function.
how_it_works: Must: the Standards bind employed and contracted auditors alike, and a contracted CAE too (Domain III and Domain IV introductions).
Should (Standard 9.3 Methodologies): the CAE keeps a documented approach for managing external service providers whenever they are used.
Must (Standard 12.3): the CAE supervises provider engagements as for staff; supervision may be delegated, accountability may not.
May (Standard 10.2): use a provider for specialist skills, special projects or whole engagements, weighing its cost and flexibility against hiring.
Must: the Standards bind contracted auditors like staff, objectivity rules included (Standard 2.2). Should (Standard 8.4): a firm that assisted the function is a doubtful external assessor.
Should (Standard 10.1): insourced or outsourced, the function still has an adequate budget approved by the board.
subtopics.example: A regional bank in Accra co-sources its IT audits with a consulting firm. The firm's lead, Kwabena, proposes skipping the bank's workpaper review to save fees. CAE Efua refuses: under the methodology for outside providers, the firm's workpapers get the same supervisory review as staff work, and Efua approves each final communication.

review: Compare provider workpapers with the function's supervision and review requirements
Trace each outsourced engagement to the CAE's approval of its results
evidence: Provider contracts setting scope, standards, access and confidentiality terms
Resumes of the provider staff assigned to each engagement
Workpapers carrying dated review by the CAE or a delegate
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive document how outside providers are chosen, supervised and reviewed, and apply it to every contract.
audit_focus.decides: The chief audit executive answers for results; the board oversees the function

subtopics.isaca_rule: Outsource the work, never the responsibility. The Standards bind contracted auditors as fully as staff; the CAE supervises their engagements and answers for conformance; the board still approves the budget.

exam_traps.trap: Once a reputable firm does the internal audit work, conformance becomes the firm's responsibility.
exam_traps.why: The CAE answers for conformance through the quality program and supervises every engagement; the board keeps its oversight role.

exam_traps.trap: An outsourced function needs no board-approved budget, because the contract fee is fixed.
exam_traps.why: Standard 10.1's considerations say the board should still approve an adequate budget, insourced or outsourced.

key_terms.definition: Hiring a provider that is not part of the organization to carry out some or all internal audit work.
An outside firm or specialist engaged to supply skills, tools or staff for internal audit work.
Sharing engagement work between the internal audit function and an outside provider.

subtopics.memory_aid: Contract the hands, keep the head: outside firms do work, the CAE answers.

subtopics.name: Monitoring Internal Audit Operations
subtopics.definition: Monitoring internal audit operations means the chief audit executive (CAE) tracking, through the year, whether the function conforms with the Standards and meets its plan, budget and objectives.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Trouble shows first as late engagements, overspent hours or thin workpapers; close watch lets the CAE fix it before an external assessor finds it.
how_it_works: Must (Standard 12.1 Internal Quality Assessment): ongoing monitoring of conformance and of progress toward performance objectives is part of the internal assessments.
Should: supervisory review of planning, workpapers and final communications is the main tool; checklists and automated workpapers help small teams.
Should (Standard 10.1): periodically compare actual spending with the budget and analyze significant variances.
May: track plan completion, engagement timeliness, budgeted against actual hours and stakeholder survey results (Standards 10.2, 12.1 considerations).
Must (Standard 12.2): measure progress toward the function's performance objectives and make an action plan for issues found; topic 3C3 holds the detail.
Must (Standard 8.3): report internal assessment results to the board and senior management at least yearly.
subtopics.example: At a hospital network in Lyon, CAE Camille reviews a monthly dashboard: plan completion, hours against budget, days from the end of fieldwork to the final communication, and survey scores. In March two engagements run 40% over their hours. Camille has the supervisors examine both work programs, finds an unclear scope in each, and adds a scope sign-off step to the methodology.

review: Sample engagements for timely supervisory review of planning and workpapers
Reperform the monthly dashboard figures from the underlying system data
Trace each monitoring issue to an action plan and its status
evidence: Time and status reports exported from the audit management system
Ledger extracts of internal audit costs by month
Review checklists signed off by supervisors
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive set a few operating measures with targets and review them with supervisors each month.
audit_focus.decides: The chief audit executive acts on results and reports to the board and senior management

subtopics.isaca_rule: Monitoring is broader than the budget: it covers conformance, plan progress, timeliness, hours and stakeholder feedback. Supervisory review is its backbone, and what it finds leads to action plans and at least yearly reporting to the board and senior management.

exam_traps.trap: Monitoring internal audit operations means checking that spending stays within the budget.
exam_traps.why: Budget variance is one measure. Ongoing monitoring also covers conformance with the Standards, supervision, plan completion, timeliness and stakeholder feedback.

exam_traps.trap: Ongoing monitoring can wait for the yearly self-assessment.
exam_traps.why: Ongoing monitoring is built into daily supervision and review; the periodic self-assessment is a separate, broader look. Both are internal assessments.

key_terms.definition: Day-to-day supervision, review and measurement, built into how the function is run, that checks conformance and progress.
The function's own check of its quality: ongoing monitoring plus periodic self-assessment, reported at least yearly.

subtopics.memory_aid: Watch the work, not just the wallet.

subtopics.name: Balancing Assurance and Advisory Work
subtopics.definition: Balancing assurance and advisory work means the chief audit executive (CAE) choosing the plan's mix of engagement types so high risks get assurance while advice still adds value.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Advisory requests are welcome and often urgent; if they quietly crowd out planned assurance in high-risk areas, the board loses assurance it believes it has.
how_it_works: Must (Standard 9.4): the plan considers the full range of services the charter allows (Standard 6.2).
Should: the methodologies say how the balance is decided, and the proposed plan labels each engagement and reserves hours for ad hoc requests (Standards 9.3, 9.4).
Must (Standard 9.4): tell the board and senior management timely of requests to swap planned assurance for advice, and why a high-risk area lacks assurance.
Must: the board approves significant plan changes; the considerations count canceling or postponing work on a significant risk as one.
Must (Standard 2.2): before assurance where the function gave advice, the CAE confirms objectivity was not impaired and staffs to manage it.
subtopics.example: Midyear at a logistics group in Rotterdam, the chief operating officer wants advice on a new warehouse system, using hours planned for assurance over customs compliance, a high-risk area. CAE Daan does not swap them quietly, but reports the conflicting demand and its effect on coverage to the board and senior management, and puts any change to the board.

review: Compare the plan's assurance and advisory mix with the strategy's intent
Trace each canceled assurance engagement to a board approval record
evidence: Minutes recording the board's vote on each plan revision
Plan versions showing engagement types and reserved hours
Memos to the board on swapped or dropped engagements
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive set out in the methodology how the assurance and advisory mix is decided and changed.
audit_focus.decides: Board approval is needed only for significant changes, such as dropping a high-risk audit

subtopics.isaca_rule: Advice is welcome, but never at the hidden cost of assurance over high risks. The CAE sets the mix by method, reports conflicting demands and uncovered high-risk areas to the board and senior management, and the board approves significant plan changes.

exam_traps.trap: Senior management asked for the advice, so the CAE may replace the planned assurance and note it at year end.
exam_traps.why: Such requests go timely to the board and senior management, and significant plan changes need board approval.

exam_traps.trap: The function should keep a fixed ratio of assurance to advisory hours every year.
exam_traps.why: No ratio is set. The mix follows the charter, the risks and the strategy, through the CAE's methodology.

key_terms.definition: Advice, started by internal auditors or on request, with no assurance given and no management responsibility taken on.
Competing requests for internal audit services between major stakeholders, such as an urgent emerging-risk request or swapping planned assurance for advice.

subtopics.memory_aid: Swap planned assurance for advice? Tell the board and senior management; if the change is significant, the board approves it.

subtopics.name: When Methodologies Need Review
subtopics.definition: Reviewing methodologies means the chief audit executive (CAE) checking whether the function's documented ways of working still fit the Standards, laws, technology and team, and updating them when not.
subtopics.why_it_matters: A manual written once drifts out of date as rules, tools and people change; auditors then follow steps that no longer conform or no longer fit the risks.
how_it_works: Must (Standard 9.3 Methodologies): the CAE sets methodologies to carry out the strategy, build the plan and conform with the Standards, and trains auditors on them.
Must: the CAE evaluates how well they work and updates them as needed, including after significant changes that affect the function.
Should: their effectiveness is reviewed during the function's quality assessments, internal and external.
Triggers named in the considerations: significant change in professional standards or guidance, laws or regulations, technology, or the function's size or makeup.
A new CAE or board chair may also warrant review. A significant methodology change may justify an earlier external assessment (Standard 8.4 considerations).
May: form follows the organization; a set of procedures, a manual or rules built into audit software can all serve.
subtopics.example: A water utility in Brisbane moves its internal audit team onto a new audit management system and absorbs the audit team of a newly acquired gas business. CAE Tane reviews the manual against both changes, rewrites the workpaper and review sections for the new system, and trains every auditor before the first engagement in the system starts.

review: Compare methodology revision dates with recent changes in standards, law and tools
Sample training records for the current methodology version
Inspect quality assessment reports for methodology gaps
evidence: Methodology change log showing versions, dates and reasons
Training attendance records or signed acknowledgments
Internal and external quality assessment conclusions on methodologies
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive review methodologies after each significant change and record the review, even when nothing changes.
audit_focus.decides: The chief audit executive sets and updates the methodologies

subtopics.isaca_rule: Methodologies are living documents. The CAE must evaluate and update them as needed, especially after significant change in standards, law, technology or the team, and must train auditors on them. Quality assessments are a natural point to test them.

exam_traps.trap: Methodologies need review only when The IIA issues new Standards.
exam_traps.why: Changes in law, technology, the function's size or makeup, and a new CAE or board chair can each warrant a review.

exam_traps.trap: Updating the manual is enough; auditors can read the changes themselves.
exam_traps.why: Standard 9.3 makes training auditors on the methodologies a requirement for the CAE.

key_terms.definition: The chief audit executive's documented way of working, which internal auditors follow.
The written collection of the function's methodologies that tells internal auditors how to work.

subtopics.memory_aid: New rules, law, tools, team or leader: reopen the manual and retrain.

topics.overview: The chief audit executive manages three kinds of resources: money, people and technology. This topic covers the budget cycle, recruiting and the roles on the team, developing, evaluating and keeping auditors, and the technology engagements need. Resources follow the strategy and plan, the board approves the budget and resource plan, and any shortfall is reported, never absorbed quietly.
can_do: Outline the budget cycle, from the plan's needs to board approval and variance review
Recognize recruiting choices and the usual roles on an internal audit team
Describe how the chief audit executive develops, evaluates, rewards and keeps auditors, including mentoring, coaching and feedback
Explain what the chief audit executive weighs before bringing new technology into audit work

subtopics.name: Budgeting for the Function
subtopics.definition: The internal audit budget is the chief audit executive's (CAE's) estimate of the money the function needs for a period, covering staff, training, travel, outside providers and technology.
subtopics.why_it_matters: The budget turns the strategy and plan into funding; a budget too small for the plan silently shrinks assurance unless its impact is reported.
how_it_works: Must (Standard 10.1 Financial Resource Management): develop a budget that lets the strategy be carried out and the plan achieved, training and technology included.
Should: follow the organization's budget process. May: keep a reserve for unforeseen but needed plan changes.
Must: seek budget approval from the board; approving the budget and resource plan is among the board's essential conditions (Standard 6.3).
Must: manage day-to-day spending in line with the budget. Should: compare planned and actual spending periodically and analyze significant variances.
Must: communicate promptly to the board and senior management the impact of insufficient funds; Standard 8.2 adds a strategy to obtain resources.
Should: if the budget sits inside another unit's budget, the CAE still knows the allocation, tracks spending and monitors sufficiency.
subtopics.example: In Santiago, a retailer's finance director cuts internal audit's travel budget by a third in September. CAE Valentina finds that four remote store audits can no longer happen, leaving two high-risk areas without assurance this year, and reports the effect promptly to the board and senior management, with options such as remote testing or restored funds.

review: Compare the approved budget with the plan's resource estimates
Trace significant budget variances to an analysis and a decision
Inspect board minutes for budget approval and shortfall reports
evidence: Signed board resolution or minutes adopting the budget
Monthly budget-to-actual reports with variance workings
CAE communications on the impact of funding cuts
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive link each budget line to the plan and report shortfalls with their effect on coverage.
audit_focus.decides: The board approves the budget; the board and senior management address shortfalls

subtopics.isaca_rule: Budget from the plan and strategy, get the board's approval, manage to it and watch the variances. When money falls short, the CAE promptly reports the impact to the board and senior management instead of quietly trimming the plan.

exam_traps.trap: The chief financial officer approves the budget, since internal audit reports administratively to finance.
exam_traps.why: The CAE must seek board approval. The administrative line may run the budget process but does not give the approval.

exam_traps.trap: After a midyear cut, the CAE drops lower-priority engagements and explains at year end.
exam_traps.why: The impact of insufficient funds is communicated promptly to the board and senior management, and significant plan changes need board approval.

key_terms.definition: The difference between planned and actual spending, analyzed when significant to decide whether the budget or plan needs adjusting.
Money or hours held back for needed plan changes nobody could foresee.

subtopics.memory_aid: Plan, price, board approves, track, tell early.

subtopics.name: Recruiting and Team Roles
subtopics.definition: Recruiting is how the chief audit executive (CAE) finds internal auditors with the competencies the strategy and plan need; team roles set who performs, supervises and leads the work.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Hiring for the wrong skills, or blurring who supervises whom, leaves gaps that training cannot close in time and weakens review of the work.
how_it_works: Must (Standard 10.2 Human Resources Management): set an approach to recruit, develop and retain qualified auditors, and strive for staff who are appropriate, sufficient and well deployed.
Should: write job descriptions with human resources, matched to Standard 3.1 and competency frameworks, and take part in recruiting events and interviews.
Should: weigh hiring against contracting, value diverse backgrounds, agree the approach with the board and senior management, plan CAE succession.
Should: work within the organization's personnel policies or public-sector rules, and tell the board and senior management if they block needed hires.
The Standards name three roles (internal auditor, engagement supervisor, CAE); other titles are local choices (competency framework guide).
The guide's example role profiles, compared below, are benchmarks, not requirements.

rows.label: Staff auditor
cells: Performs assigned tests under supervision
Basic at entry level

rows.label: Senior auditor
cells: Plans and does fieldwork with less help; may supervise staff
Intermediate in internal auditing competencies

rows.label: Lead auditor or audit manager
cells: Supervises engagements: risk assessment, scope, work program
Advanced in several subcategories

rows.label: Director or senior manager
cells: Manages projects and other auditors
Advanced in all internal auditing competencies

rows.label: Chief audit executive
cells: Leads the function and advises the board
Advanced in all, expert in most

subtopics.example: A software company in Bengaluru needs stronger data analytics in internal audit for a new public contract. CAE Priya compares competency assessments with the plan, finds no one above basic proficiency in analytics, and works with human resources on a job description for a senior specialist. Until the hire starts, Priya contracts an analytics firm.

review: Compare job descriptions with the competencies the plan needs
Trace each open role to recruiting steps and interim cover
evidence: Collective competency assessment against the plan's needs
Role specifications naming the proficiency each position requires
Resumes and contracts of staff and provider auditors
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive refresh job descriptions from a gap analysis of team competencies against the plan.
audit_focus.decides: The board approves the resource plan; the chief audit executive recruits

subtopics.isaca_rule: Recruit for the gap the strategy and plan reveal, not just to fill seats: the CAE must strive for staff who are appropriate, sufficient and well deployed. The Standards name three roles; other titles are local choices, and the framework's profiles are benchmarks.

exam_traps.trap: The Standards require set job levels such as staff, senior and manager, each with a fixed proficiency.
exam_traps.why: The Standards name only the internal auditor, engagement supervisor and CAE; the framework's role profiles are examples.

exam_traps.trap: Recruiting is the human resources department's job, so the CAE need not take part.
exam_traps.why: The considerations ask the CAE to work with human resources on job descriptions and to join recruiting activities and interviews.

key_terms.definition: How far a person has advanced in a skill or subject: basic, intermediate, advanced or expert.
Appropriate: the right mix of knowledge, skills and abilities. Sufficient: enough people and hours for the plan.

subtopics.memory_aid: Hire for the gap; three roles in the Standards, the rest are local titles.

subtopics.name: Developing, Evaluating and Keeping Auditors
subtopics.definition: People management in internal audit is how the chief audit executive (CAE) trains, evaluates, rewards and keeps internal auditors so the team's competencies keep pace with the plan.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Turnover and stale skills undo good recruiting, and badly designed ratings or bonuses can bias auditors toward pleasing the managers they audit.
how_it_works: Must (Standard 10.2): the CAE evaluates each auditor's competencies, encourages development, and helps through training, supervisory feedback or mentoring.
Must (Standard 12.3): give auditors performance feedback and chances to improve. May: yearly evaluations; the competency framework guide compares assessed proficiency with targets.
Should (Standard 10.2): pay, promotion and recognition support the function's strategic objectives; methodologies cover training and performance evaluation.
Should (Standard 2.2): avoid ratings or pay based mainly on the reviewed managers' input, on findings counts, or on cost savings imposed on the area.
Should (Standard 3.2): budget and plan training and set continuing education expectations. The competency framework guide adds comparing each auditor with role profiles for development and promotion.
Should: when staff rotate in from the business, the CAE watches for objectivity impairments and applies safeguards (Standard 10.2).

types.meaning: Specific written or spoken comments from supervisors during workpaper review and after engagements (Standards 10.2, 12.3).
Less experienced auditors follow and observe knowledgeable colleagues on real engagements (Standard 10.2 considerations).
Supervisors discuss an auditor's self-assessment and performance to agree development actions (competency framework guide).
Pay, promotion and recognition that support the strategic objectives; the CAE should avoid designs, such as findings counts, that may impair objectivity (Standards 10.2, 2.2).
KaiSip's reading: rotations, special assignments and schedules matched to skills and availability (Standards 3.2, 10.2).

subtopics.example: At an insurer in Toronto, two senior auditors resign in one year, saying they saw no path to leading engagements. CAE Morgan pairs each remaining senior with a lead auditor as mentor, sets competency targets from the team's assessments, and replaces a bonus built on findings counts with one built on review quality, timeliness and development goals.

review: Compare each development plan with the auditor's latest competency assessment
Inspect rating and bonus criteria for findings counts or reviewed managers' scores
evidence: Individual competency assessments with agreed development actions
Course completion logs for each auditor this year
Performance evaluation forms and the remuneration scheme
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive base auditor ratings and rewards on work quality, development goals and the strategy.
audit_focus.decides: The chief audit executive evaluates auditors within human resources policy

subtopics.isaca_rule: Must: assess each auditor's competencies, give performance feedback and help them develop through training, feedback or mentoring. Should: reward what the strategy needs, and avoid ratings or pay resting on findings counts or mainly on reviewed managers' views.

exam_traps.trap: Ranking auditors by the number of findings they raise rewards rigor.
exam_traps.why: The considerations of Standard 2.2 name findings-count measures as a remuneration design that may impair objectivity.

exam_traps.trap: Once auditors are certified, their professional development is their own business.
exam_traps.why: Each auditor owns their development, but the CAE must evaluate competencies and help them develop, and should budget and plan training.

key_terms.definition: Ongoing education, training and experience that keep an auditor's competencies current.
Staff from business units join internal audit for a time and then return; it brings skills but needs objectivity safeguards.

subtopics.memory_aid: Assess, feed back, develop, reward the strategy; keep findings counts out of pay.

subtopics.name: Technology for Internal Audit Work
subtopics.definition: Technological resources are the systems and tools the internal audit function uses for its own work, such as audit management software, data analytics, process mapping and collaboration tools.
subtopics.why_it_matters: The right tools let auditors test whole populations and work faster, but tools brought in without training or security review waste money or expose sensitive data.
how_it_works: Must (Standard 10.3 Technological Resources): the chief audit executive (CAE) strives to give the function technology that supports its work, and evaluates it regularly for improvements.
Must: when bringing in new technology, train auditors to use it well and work with the IT and information security functions to implement it properly.
Must: tell the board and senior management how technology limits affect the function's effectiveness or efficiency.
Should: assess feasibility, share governance, risk and control systems with other departments where sensible, and present supported funding requests for approval.
Should: plan each rollout with training, and show the board and senior management the benefits realized.
Should: identify and respond to the risks the tools bring, such as information security and the privacy of personal data.
subtopics.example: In Johannesburg, a mining group's CAE, Thabo, wants a continuous analytics tool for procurement payments. Before buying, Thabo has information security review data access and encryption, has IT plan the link to the payment system, budgets training for all six auditors, and commits to report to the board after a year on exceptions found and hours saved.

review: Compare tools in use with the technology initiatives in the strategy
Sample training records for each audit tool deployed
Inspect security reviews completed before each tool's rollout
evidence: Sign-off from the information security function before go-live
Funding requests and post-rollout benefit reports to the board
Training records for each new audit tool
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive roll out each new tool with training, a security review and a benefits report.
audit_focus.decides: The board and senior management approve technology funding requests

subtopics.isaca_rule: Technology serves the work. Before rollout, train auditors and work with IT and information security; after it, show the benefits. Tell the board and senior management when missing or weak technology limits the function.

exam_traps.trap: Independence means internal audit should install its own tools without involving IT or information security.
exam_traps.why: Standard 10.3 requires the CAE to collaborate with the IT and information security functions to implement technology properly.

exam_traps.trap: Buying the tool is the step that matters; skills follow with use.
exam_traps.why: Implementing new technology requires appropriate training for internal auditors in using it effectively.

key_terms.definition: Software that holds the plan, engagements, workpapers, review sign-offs and action tracking in one place.
Using software to examine whole sets of data for patterns, trends and exceptions.

subtopics.memory_aid: Train, secure, prove the benefit, and report the limits.

topics.topic_name: Internal audit strategy and its stakeholders
topics.overview: The internal audit strategy is the function's plan for the next few years: where it wants to be and how it will get there. This topic covers how the strategy supports the organization's own strategy and risk management, what vision and mission statements are for, resource planning that follows the strategy, and what should prompt a review.
can_do: Describe how the internal audit strategy serves the organization's objectives and its risk management
Explain what a vision statement and a mission statement each do, and which one the Standards require
Describe how resource planning follows from the strategy's objectives and initiatives
Identify the events that should prompt a review of the strategy

subtopics.name: The Internal Audit Strategy and the Organization's Strategy
subtopics.definition: The internal audit strategy is the chief audit executive's (CAE's) long-term plan of action: where the function should be in a few years and how to get there.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Without a strategy a function drifts toward work it already knows; with one, its services, skills and tools follow the organization's objectives and risks.
how_it_works: Must (Standard 9.2 Internal Audit Strategy): the CAE develops and carries out a strategy that supports the organization's strategic objectives and fits stakeholders' expectations.
Must: the strategy holds a vision, strategic objectives and supporting initiatives.
Must (Standard 9.1): the CAE first understands the organization's governance, risk management and control processes. Should: gauge how mature they are.
Should: start from the organization's strategy and the expectations of the board and senior management; a strengths and weaknesses review or a gap analysis may help.
Should: initiatives cover building auditors' competencies, technology that improves the function and other improvements, each prioritized with target dates.
Must: review the strategy with the board and senior management periodically. The Standards require review, not board approval.

rows.label: Horizon
cells: Several years, for example three to five
A period, resting on a risk assessment done at least yearly

rows.label: Contents
cells: Vision, strategic objectives, supporting initiatives
Engagements, their rationale and the resources needed

rows.label: Board's part
cells: Reviewed with the board and senior management periodically
Approved by the board, as are significant changes

rows.label: Standard
cells: Standard 9.2
Standard 9.4

subtopics.example: A public university in Valparaíso adopts a five-year plan to move most teaching online. CAE Ignacio revises the internal audit strategy: a vision of trusted adviser on digital risk, assurance over every major online system by year three, and training two auditors in IT auditing. Ignacio then reviews it with the board and senior management.

review: Compare strategic objectives with the organization's current strategic plan
Inspect board minutes for periodic strategy reviews covering initiative progress
evidence: Dated, version-controlled strategy document with each required element
Workpapers from the gap exercise that shaped the objectives
Board minutes recording each periodic review
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive map each strategic objective to an organizational objective or risk, with owners and dates.
audit_focus.decides: The chief audit executive owns the strategy and reviews it with the board

subtopics.isaca_rule: The strategy points the function at the organization's objectives and risks for the next few years; the plan picks this period's engagements. Must: a vision, objectives and initiatives, reviewed periodically with the board and senior management. Board approval is not required.

exam_traps.trap: The internal audit strategy is the annual audit plan under another name.
exam_traps.why: The strategy sets long-term direction; the plan lists the period's engagements from a risk assessment and is board-approved.

exam_traps.trap: The Standards require the board to approve the internal audit strategy.
exam_traps.why: Standard 9.2 requires periodic review with the board and senior management; approval is required for the charter, plan and budget.

key_terms.definition: The function's long-term plan of action: a vision, the objectives that reach it and the initiatives that deliver them.
Achievable targets that move the function toward its vision.
Prioritized, dated actions that deliver each strategic objective.

subtopics.memory_aid: Strategy: years, vision, reviewed with the board. Plan: this period, risks, approved by the board.

subtopics.name: Vision and Mission Statements
subtopics.definition: A vision statement describes the future the internal audit function is working toward; a mission statement, in common usage, says why the function exists and whom it serves.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Short, shared statements give auditors and stakeholders one direction and purpose, and a test for whether a new initiative belongs.
how_it_works: Must (Standard 9.2): the strategy includes a vision. Should: it describes the desired future state, for example three to five years ahead, and gives direction.
Should: the vision also inspires auditors to keep improving; strategic objectives then set achievable targets toward it.
Common usage: a mission statement says what the function does, for whom and why. The Standards neither require nor define one.
KaiSip's reading: a mission statement should stay consistent with the Purpose of Internal Auditing (Domain I) and the mandate in the board-approved charter.
The charter, not a mission statement, is the binding document: it holds the mandate, the reporting lines and the commitment to the Standards (Standard 6.2).

rows.label: Answers
cells: Where should the function be in a few years?
Why does the function exist, and for whom?

rows.label: Basis
cells: Required inside the strategy (Standard 9.2)
Common usage; not in the Standards

rows.label: Changes when
cells: The strategy is revised
KaiSip's reading: the mandate or purpose changes

subtopics.example: During a strategy workshop, the internal audit team of a shipping line in Piraeus drafts two statements. The vision: be the board's first call for insight on emerging maritime risks by 2029. The mission: give independent, risk-based assurance and advice that help the company meet its objectives. CAE Eleni checks the mission against the charter's mandate before putting both in the strategy.

review: Trace each strategic objective back to the stated vision
Read any mission statement against the scope in the charter
evidence: Strategy document in which the vision appears
Charter text with the board's approval date
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive revisit the vision whenever the strategy is revised and keep any mission statement consistent with the charter.
audit_focus.decides: The chief audit executive sets the vision and reviews it with the board

subtopics.isaca_rule: The vision is required inside the strategy and points to the future. Common usage: a mission statement says why the function exists; the Standards do not require one. KaiSip's reading: keep it within the board-approved charter's mandate.

exam_traps.trap: The Standards require every function to publish a mission statement approved by the board.
exam_traps.why: Standard 9.2 requires a vision within the strategy. The Standards do not require a mission statement; the binding document is the board-approved charter.

exam_traps.trap: The vision describes what the function does today.
exam_traps.why: The vision describes a desired future state; the strategic objectives and initiatives say how the function gets there.

key_terms.definition: The desired future state of the internal audit function, often three to five years ahead, that gives the strategy direction.
Common usage: a short statement of why the function exists, what it does and whom it serves.
The board-approved document holding the function's mandate, position and reporting lines.

subtopics.memory_aid: Vision: where we are going. Mission: why we exist. Charter: what binds us.

subtopics.name: Resource Planning That Follows the Strategy
subtopics.definition: Resource planning is the chief audit executive's (CAE's) work of matching people, skills, money and technology to the strategy and plan, and closing any gap.
subtopics.why_it_matters: A strategy without resources stays a wish; showing the gap and its cost lets the board and senior management decide on funding.
how_it_works: Must (Standard 8.2 Resources): judge whether resources suffice for the mandate and plan; if not, set a strategy to obtain them and inform the board of the impact.
Should: that strategy provides a resource plan, which may hold a budget request, staffing and technology options and a cost-benefit analysis.
May: begin with a gap analysis; The IIA's competency framework suggests assessing the team's collective competencies against the strategy.
Must (Standards 10.1, 10.2): the budget and the approach to recruiting and developing auditors serve the strategy and plan.
May: close gaps by training, guest auditors, hiring, other assurance providers, rotation or an external service provider.
Board essential conditions: approve the budget and resource plan; discuss resource sufficiency with the CAE at least yearly (Standards 6.3, 8.2).
subtopics.example: A Basel drug maker's internal audit strategy calls for assurance over AI in research within two years. CAE Lukas finds a data science gap in the team and presents three costed options to the board: train two auditors, hire a specialist, or co-source. The board approves a resource plan combining training and co-sourcing.

review: Compare each strategic objective's skill needs with assessed team skills
Trace each shortfall to a costed option put to the board
evidence: Competency inventory showing current and target proficiency
Business case papers sent to the board with each funding ask
Minutes of the yearly sufficiency discussion
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive refresh the resource plan whenever the strategy changes and tie each request to an objective.
audit_focus.decides: The board approves the resource plan; senior management helps provide resources

subtopics.isaca_rule: Plan resources from the strategy, not last year's headcount. Must: judge sufficiency and, when short, set a way to obtain resources and inform the board. Board essential condition: approve the resource plan.

exam_traps.trap: When resources fall short, the CAE trims the strategy to fit the current team, without troubling the board.
exam_traps.why: Standard 8.2 requires a strategy to obtain resources and telling the board the impact and how it will be addressed.

exam_traps.trap: Senior management approves the internal audit resource plan.
exam_traps.why: Approving the resource plan is a board essential condition; senior management works with the board to provide resources.

key_terms.definition: The plan for the people, money and technology the audit plan needs.
A comparison of what the function has with what its strategy and plan need.
An expert from elsewhere in the organization who joins an engagement to supply a missing skill.

subtopics.memory_aid: Strategy first, then the gap, then costed options for the board.

subtopics.name: Reviewing and Revising the Strategy
subtopics.definition: Strategy review is the chief audit executive's (CAE's) periodic check, with the board and senior management, that the internal audit strategy still fits the organization and is on track.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Organizations change faster than five-year plans; a strategy never revisited keeps building skills and services for risks that have moved on.
how_it_works: Must (Standard 9.2): review the strategy with the board and senior management periodically; the Standards set no fixed interval.
Should: adjust the strategy whenever the organization's strategic objectives or stakeholders' expectations change.
Prompts named in the considerations: a change in the organization's strategy, or in how mature its governance, risk management and control processes are.
More prompts: new policies, laws or regulations; a change in the board, senior management or the CAE; and results of internal or external assessments.
Should: each review discusses progress on the initiatives. May: set a timeline and performance measures to track them (Standard 12.2).
subtopics.example: A telecom group in Nairobi merges with a rival, and a new audit committee chair joins the board. CAE Wanjiru does not wait for the planned three-year review. Wanjiru reassesses the strategy's objectives against the merged company's priorities, reports progress on the current initiatives, and discusses a revised version with the new chair and senior management.

review: Compare strategy review dates with major organizational and leadership changes
Inspect review records for progress on each supporting initiative
evidence: Board minutes of strategy reviews covering initiative progress
Dated strategy versions with reasons for each revision
Quality assessment results used in the latest revision
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive list strategy review triggers in the methodology and record the outcome of each review.
audit_focus.decides: The chief audit executive revises the strategy after review with the board

subtopics.isaca_rule: Review the strategy with the board and senior management periodically, and sooner when the organization's strategy, risk maturity, rules, leaders or quality assessment results change. A strategy set once and left alone is a gap.

exam_traps.trap: A strategy is reviewed only when its planned term ends.
exam_traps.why: It should be adjusted whenever strategic objectives or stakeholder expectations change; new leaders, new laws and assessment results may prompt an earlier review.

exam_traps.trap: A change of chief audit executive has no bearing on the strategy.
exam_traps.why: A new CAE, like new board members or senior managers, is one of the events that can call for an earlier review.

key_terms.definition: A periodic discussion with the board and senior management of whether the strategy still fits and how its initiatives are progressing.
How developed and dependable the organization's processes for finding and managing risk are.

subtopics.memory_aid: New strategy, rules, leaders or assessment results: reopen the internal audit strategy.

topics.topic_name: Chief audit executive reporting and relationships
topics.overview: The chief audit executive is the function's voice to the board and senior management. This topic covers building relationships through formal and informal contact, presenting the plan and its changes, raising independence concerns and risks accepted beyond appetite, and reporting themes, organization-level conclusions and the function's quality and performance.
can_do: Explain why the chief audit executive needs both formal reports and informal contact with stakeholders
Describe how the plan and its later changes reach the board and senior management, and who approves them
Recognize the route for independence concerns and for risk accepted beyond appetite
Recognize what reports on themes, organization-level conclusions, quality results and performance measures must contain

subtopics.name: Formal Reports and Informal Contact
subtopics.definition: Stakeholder communication is the chief audit executive's (CAE's) mix of formal reports and meetings and informal contact with the board, management, regulators and other assurance providers.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Formal channels give the board a record for oversight; informal contact builds the trust that brings out concerns people would not raise in a meeting.
how_it_works: Must (Standard 11.1): the CAE sets an approach for earning key stakeholders' trust and building relationships, and promotes formal and informal communication.
Must (Standard 8.1): give the board the information it needs for oversight, whether the board asks for it or the CAE judges it valuable.
Should: agree with the board what counts as significant, the format and the frequency of formal reports, and confirm them periodically.
Must (Standard 6.3): coordinate board communications with senior management, so reporting is neither redundant nor conflicting.
Should: meet the board without senior management at least yearly, quarterly as leading practice, and brief senior management on these discussions unless inappropriate.
Should: attend board and key committee meetings and keep regular informal contact; meeting executives one to one builds relationships. May: rotate auditors to protect objectivity.
subtopics.example: In Kraków, CAE Zofia reports to the audit committee each quarter, holds a private session after each meeting, and hears of a supplier problem over coffee with the chief risk officer. After one private session on the chief commercial officer's expense claims, Zofia does not brief senior management, because the matter concerns one of its members.

review: Compare board records with the agreed reporting frequency and content
Inspect private session records and the notices given to senior management
evidence: Board agendas and minutes showing CAE reports and private sessions
Agreed matrix of what is reported, to whom and how often
Stakeholder relationship plan and meeting notes
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive agree a reporting matrix with the board and confirm periodically that it meets the board's needs.
audit_focus.decides: The board sets its expectations on frequency, escalation criteria and process

subtopics.isaca_rule: Report formally, relate informally. Must: give the board what it needs for oversight, not only what it asks for. Should: meet it privately at least yearly and tell senior management about those sessions unless inappropriate.

exam_traps.trap: The CAE reports only what the board asks for, to respect its agenda.
exam_traps.why: Standard 8.1 also covers information the CAE judges valuable for the board's oversight.

exam_traps.trap: Private sessions with the board must always be kept from senior management.
exam_traps.why: The CAE should brief senior management on these discussions unless that would be inappropriate, as when the matter concerns a senior manager's conduct.

key_terms.definition: A meeting of the board and the chief audit executive with no senior management in the room.
Regular, unscheduled contact, such as one-to-one conversations, that builds trust and understanding between formal reports.

subtopics.memory_aid: Formal for the record, informal for the trust.

subtopics.name: Communicating the Plan and Its Changes
subtopics.definition: Plan communication is how the chief audit executive (CAE) presents the internal audit plan, its link to the organization's strategy, and later changes to the board and senior management.
subtopics.why_it_matters: The board can only approve and rely on a plan it understands; an unreported change leaves it believing risks are covered when they are not.
how_it_works: Must (Standard 9.4): ground the plan in a documented assessment, at least yearly, of the organization's risks, objectives and strategies, with board and senior management input.
Must: discuss the plan and significant interim changes with the board and senior management; the board approves the plan and significant changes.
Must (Standard 8.1): report the plan, the budget and later significant revisions to the board and senior management.
Must (Standard 9.4): communicate timely resource limits on coverage, why a high-risk area lacks an assurance engagement, conflicting demands, and scope or access limits.
Should: agree criteria for significant changes, such as canceling or postponing work on significant risks, and write them into the methodologies.
Should: if an urgent risk forces a change before a board meeting, inform the board at once and seek formal approval soon after.
subtopics.example: Facing a wave of cyberattacks in May, the CAE of Montevideo's city government, Lucía, moves two auditors from a fleet maintenance review to urgent cybersecurity work. The agreed criteria make this a significant change, so Lucía informs the audit committee and the city manager that day and seeks formal approval in June.

review: Trace each significant plan change to board approval or immediate notice
Compare each engagement's rationale with the organization's strategies and risks
evidence: Minutes and resolutions recording each plan approval
Risk ranking workpapers supporting each engagement choice
Protocol document for handling urgent plan changes
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive agree with the board which plan changes are significant and how urgent ones are approved.
audit_focus.decides: Approval sits with the board alone

subtopics.isaca_rule: The CAE discusses the plan with the board and senior management; the board approves it and its significant changes. An urgent change is told to the board at once and approved formally soon after.

exam_traps.trap: Senior management approves the plan, and the board is informed.
exam_traps.why: The board approves the plan and significant changes; senior management is consulted and gives input.

exam_traps.trap: Significant plan changes can wait for the year-end activity report.
exam_traps.why: Significant changes need board approval; an urgent one should be told to the board at once, with approval soon after.

key_terms.definition: The list of engagements internal audit intends to carry out in a period, chosen by risk.
A plan change meeting criteria agreed by the CAE, the board and senior management, such as canceling or postponing work on a significant risk.

subtopics.memory_aid: Discuss with both, approved by the board; urgent change: tell now, approve soon.

subtopics.name: Raising Independence Threats and Risk Exposures
subtopics.definition: Raising concerns means the chief audit executive (CAE) taking threats to independence, and risk accepted beyond appetite, to senior management and the board by the set routes.
subtopics.why_it_matters: These are the matters the board most needs to hear and management least wants raised; a clear route protects the function and lets the board act.
how_it_works: Must (Standard 7.1): confirm independence to the board at least yearly, with any possible impairments and the safeguards used.
Must (Standards 7.1, 8.1): discuss roles that could impair independence with the board and senior management, and report potential impairments to both.
Must (Standard 11.5): when management accepts risk beyond the risk appetite or risk tolerance, discuss it with senior management; if unresolved, escalate to the board.
Should: first raise it with the responsible management. The CAE does not resolve the risk (topics 3D6, 3D8).
Must (Standard 8.1): when a disagreement with senior management may affect the function's work, give the board the facts to decide whether to intervene.
Board essential condition (Standard 8.1): set with the CAE the criteria and process for escalating matters, such as significant risks beyond the board's risk tolerance.

rows.label: Trigger
cells: A role, pressure, budget cut or access limit that may impair independence
Management accepts risk above the risk appetite or risk tolerance

rows.label: Who hears it
cells: The board and senior management (Standards 7.1, 8.1)
Should: the responsible management. Must: senior management (Standard 11.5)

rows.label: The board's part
cells: Receives the yearly confirmation; works out safeguards
Receives it if senior management leaves it unresolved, and decides

subtopics.example: At a Manila power utility, CAE Rizal is asked to run treasury for six months. Before accepting, Rizal explains to the board and senior management how the role could impair independence, proposes outside treasury assurance during the role and 12 months after, and agrees a handback plan.

review: Inspect board minutes for the yearly independence confirmation and impairments
Trace risk acceptance cases from management to senior management to the board
evidence: Board minutes recording the independence confirmation and safeguards
Escalation records naming the risk, the concern and who accepted it
Escalation protocol document approved by the board
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive agree escalation criteria with the board and document each independence or risk acceptance discussion.
audit_focus.decides: The board agrees safeguards and decides on unresolved risk acceptance

subtopics.isaca_rule: Independence concerns go to the board and senior management, with a yearly confirmation to the board. Risk accepted beyond appetite: must go to senior management, then the board if unresolved; the responsible manager first is a should.

exam_traps.trap: An independence concern is raised with senior management, who decide whether the board needs to know.
exam_traps.why: Potential impairments are reported to the board and senior management, and independence is confirmed to the board at least yearly.

exam_traps.trap: If senior management leaves an unacceptable risk unresolved, the CAE orders it fixed.
exam_traps.why: Resolving the risk is not the CAE's job: the CAE escalates to the board, which decides how to address it.

key_terms.definition: How much risk, and which kinds, an organization is prepared to take for its strategy.
The band of results around an objective that the organization can live with.

subtopics.memory_aid: Independence: board and senior management. Risk beyond appetite: senior management, then the board.

subtopics.name: Themes, Organization-Level Conclusions and Quality Results
subtopics.definition: Function-level reporting is the chief audit executive's (CAE's) reporting to the board and senior management on patterns across engagements, any organization-level conclusion, and the function's own quality.
subtopics.why_it_matters: One engagement shows one area; patterns across many show where control is really weak, and quality reports show whether the board can trust the function.
how_it_works: Must (Standard 11.3 Communicating Results): communicate results to the board and senior management periodically and per engagement, as their expectations require.
Must: when the CAE identifies themes, such as a shared root cause, communicate them timely with insights, advice or conclusions.

Must: an organization-level conclusion, when required, rests on several engagements and states the request, criteria, scope with limitations and period, supporting information and any reliance on other providers.
Must (Standard 8.3): report internal assessment results at least yearly and external results when complete: conformance, performance objectives and plans for any gaps.
Must (Standard 12.1): share self-assessment results and action plans. Should (Standard 12.2): track and report performance action plans; see topics 3C1 and 3C3.

rows.label: Themes across engagements
cells: Timely, once identified
Standard 11.3

rows.label: Organization-level conclusion
cells: When law, industry or stakeholders require one
Standard 11.3

rows.label: Internal assessment results
cells: At least yearly
Standards 8.3, 12.1

rows.label: External assessment results
cells: When completed
Standards 8.3, 8.4

rows.label: Performance objectives
cells: Approved by the board at least yearly
Standards 8.3, 12.2

subtopics.example: Across six branch audits in a year, a Halifax credit union's internal auditors keep finding manual overrides of loan limits, each traced to the same outdated lending system. CAE Jordan reports the theme, its shared root cause and advice to the board and senior management in the next quarterly report, instead of leaving it scattered.

review: Compare findings across engagements for shared root causes left unreported
Inspect quality reports for conformance, objectives and improvement plans
evidence: Quarterly board packs with cross-engagement analysis
Assessor reports and the CAE's dated responses
Performance reports against board-approved objectives
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive track findings across engagements by root cause and report themes in each periodic report.
audit_focus.decides: The board approves the function's yearly objectives and its responses to external assessments

subtopics.isaca_rule: Look across engagements, not only within them: themes reach the board and senior management timely. An organization-level conclusion needs criteria, scope and support from several engagements. Quality results go to the board at least yearly, with plans to fix gaps.

exam_traps.trap: Every CAE must give a yearly conclusion on the whole organization's controls.
exam_traps.why: Such a conclusion is given when law, industry rules or stakeholders require it, and must then be scoped and supported.

exam_traps.trap: Internal assessment results go to the board only when they show problems.
exam_traps.why: Standard 8.3 requires internal assessment results at least yearly, whatever they show, with improvement plans where applicable.

key_terms.definition: Patterns or trends across several engagements, such as a shared root cause or a practice worth spreading.
The CAE's judgment on governance, risk management or control for a business unit or the whole organization, drawn from several engagements.

subtopics.memory_aid: Themes timely, organization-level conclusions when required, quality at least yearly.

key_terminologies.Chief audit executive (CAE): The head of the internal audit function, whatever the job title.
key_terminologies.Board: The highest governing body, such as the directors or audit committee; where several govern, the body (or bodies) empowered to give internal audit its mandate.
key_terminologies.Senior management: The top executives, usually including the chief executive officer, who answer to the board.
key_terminologies.Essential conditions: Board and senior management activities, not requirements on them, that Domain III lists as necessary for an effective internal audit function.
key_terminologies.Internal audit strategy: The function's long-term plan of action: a vision, the objectives that reach it and the initiatives that deliver them.
key_terminologies.Vision: The desired future state of the internal audit function, often three to five years ahead, that gives the strategy direction.
key_terminologies.Mission statement: Common usage: a short statement of why the function exists, what it does and whom it serves.
key_terminologies.Methodologies: The chief audit executive's documented way of working, which internal auditors follow.
key_terminologies.Internal audit plan: The list of engagements internal audit intends to carry out in a period, chosen by risk.
key_terminologies.Significant change: A plan change meeting criteria agreed by the CAE, the board and senior management, such as canceling or postponing work on a significant risk.
key_terminologies.Resource plan: The plan for the people, money and technology the audit plan needs.
key_terminologies.Budget variance: The difference between planned and actual spending, analyzed when significant to decide whether the budget or plan needs adjusting.
key_terminologies.Outsourcing: Hiring a provider that is not part of the organization to carry out some or all internal audit work.
key_terminologies.External service provider: An outside firm or specialist engaged to supply skills, tools or staff for internal audit work.
key_terminologies.Co-sourcing: Sharing engagement work between the internal audit function and an outside provider.
key_terminologies.Guest auditor: An expert from elsewhere in the organization who joins an engagement to supply a missing skill.
key_terminologies.Rotational staffing: Staff from business units join internal audit for a time and then return; it brings skills but needs objectivity safeguards.
key_terminologies.Proficiency level: How far a person has advanced in a skill or subject: basic, intermediate, advanced or expert.
key_terminologies.Ongoing monitoring: Day-to-day supervision, review and measurement, built into how the function is run, that checks conformance and progress.
key_terminologies.Private session: A meeting of the board and the chief audit executive with no senior management in the room.
key_terminologies.Themes: Patterns or trends across several engagements, such as a shared root cause or a practice worth spreading.
key_terminologies.Organization-level conclusion: The CAE's judgment on governance, risk management or control for a business unit or the whole organization, drawn from several engagements.
key_terminologies.Risk appetite: How much risk, and which kinds, an organization is prepared to take for its strategy.
key_terminologies.Risk tolerance: The band of results around an objective that the organization can live with.
key_terminologies.Advisory services: Advice, started by internal auditors or on request, with no assurance given and no management responsibility taken on.
